I'm trying something new here, trying to help you all learn some fundamentals of physics. Not sure how regular this will be, we'll see. I'd like to focus on basic but far-reaching concepts, rather than esoteric oddities. So today I'll tell you all something about the laws of thermodynamics.

1. Energy is conserved

There are several equivalent ways to state this, but we're keeping it simple. What this means is that if you have a closed system, the energy content of that system will remain constant. It also means that for any point, the local energy density will go up if there is more energy flowing in than flowing out, or vice versa.

This law is based on Noether's theorem, one of the most fundamental theorems in all of theoretical physics. Basically, it states that if the laws of physics do not depend on time, that means energy is conversed. Likewise, if the laws of physics do not depend on space, that means momentum is conserved. Think about it this way: if it doesn't matter where you are, there is nothing inherent in the physics of the universe that will make you move faster or slower.

2. In a closed system, entropy will never decrease

For this, we need to understand what entropy is and why it is something that tends to go up. I'll give four different explanations for entropy and show that they are all equivalent.

1. Entropy is a measure of disorder.

I actually don't like this explanation of entropy, because it's a poor analogy and leads to faulty leaps of logic. But it's not technically incorrect and it's wildly popular, so I'm including it. You might be able to see a well-ordered structure like a neatly stacked pyramid of oranges as a low-entropy state, while them all rolling around randomly on the floor as a high entropy state. Why is something for which we actually need the other two.

2. Entropy is a measure of how many degrees of freedom that energy is spread over

This is a bit more technical, but nothing you clever goats can't handle. Think of a degree of freedom as a way in which a system can trap energy. A classic example is a freely bouncing basketball. The ball's useful energy has only one degree of freedom: the height of its bounce. The higher it bounces, the more energy it holds. The floor, on the other hand, has an incredibly large amount of degrees of freedom: every single atom in the floor that the basketball bounces on can get bumped on and start vibrating, sapping a little energy from the basketball and storing it as heat.

This is the fundamental difference between energy as work and energy as heat. Work is energy in very few degrees of freedom, directed and useful. Heat is energy spread over a huge number of degrees of freedom, it is random and useless. So every time the basketball bounces, the work energy bleeds off into heat as vibrations in the floor, vibrations in the basketball, sound waves in the air, etc.

The second law states that energy will always dissipate towards as many degrees of freedom as it can go, diffusing as much as it can.

3. Entropy is a measure of information content

When you know the previous definition, this one is easy to understand. If you're trying to describe the exact state of a system of oranges in a room, it's short and easy to say "They're stacked in a perfect pyramid in the northwest corner of the room, 20 on each side.". This is highly organized (see the first definition again?), the system is not employing its degrees of freedom at all (it's just crammed in the corner). So this is easy to describe and define.

Now imagine that someone pulled out a few from the base and they all go rolling over the floor. Describe that state exactly. One orange is 21cm from the east wall, 14cm from the north wall, rolling in the south direction with a velocity of ... And you go on and on for each one. This takes forever, there is an insane amount of information needed to be specified to define it exactly. This is why it's a high entropy state, you need a lot of information to define it.

4. Entropy is a measure of number of microstates

And now you're ready to understand the definition in terms of microstates and macrostates. A microstate is one highly specified state of a system. A macrostate is a state of the system which you can describe shortly. In the example of the oranges, there are two macrostates: pyramid and mess. The macrostate "pyramid" has only one microstate and has low entropy. The macrostate "mess" has many many microstates (the 34th orange might be rolling a little more to the left or to the right), it has high entropy.

Microstates and degrees of freedom are related, a system with many easily accessible degrees of freedom will easily allow a macrostate with many microstates.

You might be able to get a feeling now for why the second law holds. A system will tend towards a state with many microstates, employing as many degrees of freedom as possible, maximizing its hidden information content, becoming maximally disorded. And the only way to make it ordered, to stuff the energy back into few degrees of freedoms, reducing the number of microstates, is to expend energy on it.

Got it? On to the last one.

3. You cannot reach absolute zero in finitely many steps

This one is easy to give a rigorous and intuitive explanation for. But consider it like this. To lower a system's temperature, you have to try to get it to give up all its entropy. So you have to expend energy for some of that energy in there to leave the system into something you are trying to make more enticing for the energy to go into. But the colder a system is, the more degrees of freedom it will have available to suck energy in from its surroundings. So you have to try extremely hard to not let that happen, working harder and harder to suck every last bit of energy from every last degree of freedom. Eventually, you can get arbitrarily close to absolute zero, but you'll never reach it.

In a more mathematical way, the way you get something to cool down, you actually don't have to think about lowering its temperature T, but raising its coldness 1/T. This makes it much more intuitive why you can't reach absolute zero, because you have to push its coldness 1/T up to infinity.
